notes.meaning: God sets up a courtroom and calls the faraway nations to it. "Islands" means distant lands beyond the sea. They are told to be quiet so God can be heard, and then to gather their best arguments and speak. God is not afraid of a fair trial.

God asks a question: who stirred up this conqueror from the east and gave him victory over nations and kings? Many say it is Cyrus, the Persian king who would later free the Jews. It is told as if it had already happened, because it is so sure. Others say it is Abraham, who was called from the east and beat four kings to rescue Lot. Either way, the conqueror moves quickly and safely, even through lands he had never walked, because God is behind him.

God gives the answer Himself: He did this. He has called every generation into being since the beginning, and He guides all of history. "The first and the last" means He was there before everything and will be there at the end. He never changes.
The far-off nations see what God is doing, and they tremble. They are afraid the same disaster will fall on them. So they come together to find help.

Their plan is sad and a little funny. Instead of turning to God, they cheer each other on to make new idols. One worker urges on another, they say the job looks good, and they nail the idol down so it won't fall over. Matthew Henry notes that if people urge each other on in wrong, God's servants should even more urge each other on in serving Him.

"But you, Israel" is very different. Israel is God's servant, chosen by Him. That choice was a gift of grace, meaning kindness they did not earn. They come from Abraham, whom God calls "My friend", a very high honor. So they should not copy the idol-making of the nations.

God reminds them how He brought them from far away. This most likely looks back to Abraham being called from distant Ur. Some take it as the people being brought out of Egypt. God chose them and did not throw them away, even though they often let Him down.

God speaks tenderly: do not fear, for I am with you. He promises to make the weak strong, to help, and to hold them up. His "right hand of righteousness" means His hand that keeps every promise He has made. Believers may still feel afraid at times, but this promise helps them stand firm.

Those who rage against God's people will end in shame. They will vanish so fully that you could look for them and not find them. God's people should not expect a life with no enemies. They also should not pay back evil for evil. They can wait for God's time.

God promises to take His people by the right hand. He is like a guide who leads them and lifts them up when they stumble. Again He says, "Do not fear, I will help you." The promise rests on who He is, the first and the last.

God calls Israel a "worm", small, weak, and stepped on by everyone. He says it with pity, not scorn. They are worms, not snakes. Jesus used the same word for Himself in Psalm 22:6. God is their Redeemer, the one who buys back and sets free His people.

A threshing sledge was a heavy farm tool with sharp teeth that crushed grain. God will make weak Israel like that tool, able to crush "mountains", meaning powerful enemies. The point is not to stir up revenge. It shows what God will do. And the victory leads to joy in the Lord, not pride. Many see it fulfilled in the triumph of the gospel of Christ.

The poor and needy are first of all the exiles far from home in Babylon. They are parched, with no water in sight. God promises to answer them and never leave them. Many also apply this to anyone whose soul is thirsty and who cries out to God.

God will make rivers flow on bare hills and turn desert into pools. This recalls how He gave Israel water in the wilderness after Egypt. God is not limited by the normal order of nature. Many also see here the "living water" of the Holy Spirit that Jesus promised (John 7:38-39).

God will plant tall, shady trees in the desert so travelers have shelter from the heat. We are not sure exactly which trees some of these names mean. It pictures God's rich and many-sided kindness. The goal is that everyone will see and understand that God's own hand did this.
The court opens again. God, the "King of Jacob", dares the idols and their followers to bring their strongest reasons. He stands up for His people against the gods of the nations.

Here is the test: tell us what will happen, near or far. Or explain the past. Only the true God truly knows the future. Then the idols are told to "do good or evil", that is, show any sign of life or power at all. "Evil" here means trouble or punishment, not wrongdoing.
The verdict comes. The idols are nothing, and what they do is worthless. Choosing them is "detestable", something God hates. Making gods of our own choosing is the root of false worship.

God has stirred up a conqueror from the north and the east. Most take this to be Cyrus, who led Medes (north) and Persians (east). He "calls on My name" when he later honors Israel's God in his decree to free the Jews (Ezra 1:2). He will trample rulers like a potter treading clay. Some older writers see Christ pictured here too. Others take "north" to mean Babylon.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some think this part of Isaiah was written later, during the exile in Babylon. They point to a Persian word used here for "rulers" as a clue.

notes.meaning: Did any idol announce this ahead of time, so people could say, "That was true"? No one did. None of their gods or fortune-tellers said a word about it.

God was the first to tell Zion, "Look, here they come!" He sent messengers with good news through His prophets. That news was that the exiles would come home. Many also see a pointer to the good news of the gospel.
God looks among the idols, and there is no one to answer. They have no wise advice and nothing to say. They lose the case because they stay silent.
The final ruling is that the idols are a delusion and their works are nothing. Their images are as empty as the wind. The word for "empty" is the same one used for the shapeless earth in Genesis 1:2.
